title: Rolling upgrade GPU OOM sleuth playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for triaging nondeterministic GPU OOMs that appear during rolling upgrades of private deployments (VPC / on-prem). Focus is on upgrades where only a subset of nodes are updated and traffic is shifted, and where OOMs are observed on some pods after a rollout step.

Scope / when to use:
- Rolling upgrades of runtime / model-serving agent or GPU driver updates.
- Failures that show up as sudden per-pod memory spikes or OOMKilled events post-upgrade step.
- Applies to Dedicated/Private clusters using Kubernetes + GPU nodes (NVIDIA) and Redwood runtime.

Quick triage checklist (5–10 min):
- Confirm symptoms: kubectl get pods -n redwood --field-selector=status.phase!=Succeeded -o wide | grep OOMKilled
- Check node GPU memory usage: kubectl top node <node> --use-protocol-buffers OR nvidia-smi -L (on node) then nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -l 1
- Inspect pod logs and container OOM reason: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n redwood && kubectl logs <pod> -n redwood --previous
- Look for sudden kernel selection / quantization warnings in runtime logs (llama/cuda kernels).
- Verify whether drain/cordon was used correctly for the node that upgraded.

Hypotheses to consider (ordered by frequency seen):
1) Incompatible CUDA / driver mismatch after node upgrade causing memory accounting differences (driver reports lower available memory).
2) Runtime changed kernel / workspace allocation heuristics in the new version (e.g., larger default KV cache reservation or alignment changes).
3) Model artifact changed (new weights, different tokenizer) causing longer prefix or larger cache usage per request.
4) Sidecars / monitoring agents introduced background GPU usage (eBPF or profiler libs hooking into libcuda).
5) Stale pods not fully drained from previous version that continue to accept traffic and hold KV cache leading to memory fragmentation.
6) Excessive batch coalescing by the new autoscaler or batching config leading to larger transient memory peaks.

Detailed investigation steps (30–90 min):
A. Correlate timeline
- Use rollout timestamps: kubectl rollout status deploy/redwood-runtime -n redwood --watch=false and kubectl get rs -n redwood -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.metadata.creationTimestamp}\n'
- Match the node upgrade time (cloud/terraform apply time) with pod restarts and OOM events.

B. Node-level checks (SSH to node if on-prem or use cloud console):
- nvidia-smi -q | head -n 80 -> check driver/driver version, persistence mode, ECC errors.
- dmesg | tail -n 200 -> look for gpu related kernel messages, out-of-memory kworker messages, i915 errors (if integrated GPUs present).
- Check cgroup memory usage and limits: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods.slice/... (or use kubectl exec to run free/ps aux inside node agent).

C. Container/pod checks:
- kubectl exec -n redwood <pod> -- bash -c "ps aux | grep redwood-runtime" and check resident set size (RSS) for processes.
- If using our runtime image, check environment variables related to cache: REDWOOD_KV_MAX_BYTES, REDWOOD_CACHE_MODE, REDWOOD_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS.
- kubectl exec <pod> -- nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv -l 1 (if container has nvidia-smi).

D. Runtime logs to look for (search patterns):
- "alloc failed" | "OutOfMemory" | "cudaMalloc" | "failed to allocate"
- "KV cache reserve" | "batch_coalesce size" | "kernel fallback"
- Example suspicious log snippet:
  [2026-02-28T03:12:21Z] WARN runtime.memory: failed to allocate 512MB for kv-cache; attempting compaction -> fallback to full model reload
- If logs mention fallback vs kernel mismatch, note which kernel and model version.

E. Quick smoke tests to reproduce locally (prefer staging):
- Pin exactly the runtime image + model sha used in the failing pod and run a single replica on a node with similar GPU type and memory.
- Recreate a high-concurrency burst: curl -sS -X POST ... loop 50 times to simulate batch peaks and watch nvidia-smi logging.

Mitigations and short-term workarounds (fastest to deploy):
- Roll back runtime image to previous version on a small percentage (10%) of nodes to test if OOMs disappear (use canary).
- Temporarily reduce per-request token limits or reduce max batch tokens via route config to lower peak memory.
- Disable aggressive batching / set REDWOOD_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS=2048 (example) and restart pods on affected nodes.
- If driver mismatch suspected, roll driver backwards on one node and confirm OOM behavior.
- Cordon nodes that completed upgrade and route traffic away until root cause is found.

Terraform / rollout notes (practical tips):
- Pin TF module versions for node images and GPU drivers. Example: terraform module "node_pool" { source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//gke-node-pool?ref=v1.9.2" }
- Add a mandatory pause after each node pool upgrade step in the pipeline: sleep 300s and run smoke checks before continuing cluster-wide.
- Make node auto-scaling conservative during upgrades: set min/max to current capacity and avoid parallel replacements across AZs.
- Ensure node pool uses a lifecycle pre-stop hook that waits for in-flight requests to drain (graceful terminationSeconds > 120).

Recommended smoke tests to gate each upgrade step (script-friendly):
1) sanity-pod-start: schedule a tiny test pod with runtime image and run a short identity inference. Pass if exit code 0.
2) gpu-memory-stability: run a 60s loop that invokes a 2-token completion at T=0 and then a 1024-token completion; accept if peak GPU memory increase < 60% of device memory.
3) batch-peak-sim: fire 40 concurrent small requests and verify no single pod exceeds memory threshold.
4) metrics-check: scrape Prometheus for redwood_runtime_memory_bytes_used and ensure no pod crosses 85% of capacity for >30s.

Smoke test commands (examples):
- kubectl run sanity --image=gcr.io/redwood/runtime:staging --rm -n redwood --command -- /bin/sh -c "python -c 'import requests;print(requests.post(\"http://localhost:8080/generate\", json={\"prompt\":\"hi\"}).status_code)'"
- python scripts/gpu_stress_test.py --host <node-ip> --runtime-image gcr.io/redwood/runtime:vX.Y --concurrency 40 --payload-prompt-file tests/payloads/long_prompt.txt

Longer-term root causes we've observed and recommended engineering actions:
- Memory accounting drift after driver updates: add a driver-version gating test that measures baseline nvidia-smi reported free memory against host's cgroup limits before rollout.
- Runtime kernel fallback path increases memory: add unit tests that simulate kernel fallback and measure cache reservation differences.
- Batch coalescing heuristics: instrument the batching code to emit per-batch-token histograms and integrate into console dashboards for post-upgrade regression detection.
- Invisible profiler sidecar hooks: standardize base image to exclude any profiler libs (LD_PRELOAD checks in entrypoint) and hard-fail if detected.

Rollforward plan (if root cause confirmed and fix exists):
1) Build a patch image with conservative cache reservation + safer kernel selection flag.
2) Deploy as a canary to a single node pool, run full smoke tests above.
3) If green for 30m and Prometheus shows no >80% memory for any pod, continue to next pool with 15-minute pauses between pools.
4) If regressions reappear, automatically revert clusters to previous stable TF node image via terraform state rollback or by scaling up old node pool and draining new one.

Rollback plan (fastest):
- Use existing terraform module to create a new node pool with the old AMI/image + driver version, cordon and drain upgraded nodes, scale traffic down from updated pool and scale up old pool.
- Example TF snippet for fast rollback: terraform apply -var='node_pool_image=stable-202601' -target=module.node_pool.rollback
- Important: ensure node labels and taints for routing are equivalent so the router will serve traffic from rollback pool without configuration changes.

Postmortem / info to collect before closing incident:
- Pod and node timestamps for first OOM and last healthy period.
- Runtime version, model sha, kernel selection flags, and environment variables (REDWOOD_*).
- nvidia-smi logs + dmesg from affected nodes (compressed) and container logs (previous and current).
- Terraform plan logs and commit/PR that triggered the upgrade.
- Prometheus metrics for memory and request latency for 3 hours before and after rollout.

Notes for SRE / infra playbook addition:
- Add a pre-upgrade probe that runs gpu-memory-stability across representative instance types before any TF apply that changes driver/runtime.
- Automate node cordon/drain and smoke test script in CI pipeline (fail fast on OOM thresholds).
- Document known-good driver/runtime combinations in a compatibility matrix file in repo infra/docs/driver_compat.md.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Get OOMKilled pods and timestamps: kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=OOMKilled -o wide | sort -k1,1
- Dump last 500 lines of runtime log: kubectl logs deploy/redwood-runtime -n redwood --tail=500 > /tmp/runtime-tail.log
- Grab nvidia-smi loop on node (SSH): while true; do date; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,index,name,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv; sleep 5; done >> /tmp/nvidia-loop.log &
- TF note: keep module version pin close to node image lifecycle, and include a one-step TF target for rollback to previous image.

Open questions / TODOs in doc:
- Add an automated Prometheus alert playbook snippet for "GPU memory > 85% for 30s" mapped to a runbook link.
- Build a lightweight synthetic load harness that can be run as a Kubernetes Job during upgrades.
- Coordinate with model-onboarding to avoid large tokenizer/model changes on same day as infra upgrades.

End of working playbook. This doc is a living draft — please add concrete command snippets and TF module references from the last upgrade that triggered PD-3142.
